title: Koinonia: every newcomer heard, in their own language

lines.text: Every Sunday, someone slips into the back pew with something heavy to carry.
The service is in a language they don't speak. So they stay silent.
In a university town like Camerino, in Italy, students from many countries worship beside local families.
Translation apps help them hear the sermon. Nothing helps them be heard.
And when a request does arrive in Chinese or Spanish, the care team can't read it, or pastes it, names and all, into a public chatbot.
Koinonia is a two-way pastoral care bridge.
lines.say: Koy-noh-nee-ah is a two-way pastoral care bridge.

lines.text: A newcomer asks in their language. A pastor answers in theirs. And a person approves every word.
It starts with a card in the pew. No app. No account.
One tap, and the whole page speaks their language. Arabic reads right to left.
In Italian, the homily is read aloud in a native voice.
Lucía arrived from Bogotá three weeks ago. She writes in Spanish.
As she types, her name and her number are removed, right on her phone. They never leave it.
She sends it, and gets a private code. Nothing else.
At the parish, the request is already waiting, in English.
Claude writes a short summary, suggests a psalm and a group, and drafts a reply for the pastor to make their own.
Then Koinonia translates the reply into Spanish, and translates it back with a separate call that never saw the original.
lines.say: Then Koy-noh-nee-ah translates the reply into Spanish, and translates it back with a separate call that never saw the original.

lines.text: Meaning kept. Only now does Approve unlock.
The AI drafts. A pastor decides.
Lucía opens her code. The reply is in Spanish, approved by name, with a psalm, and an invitation.
Tuesday night, the students' group. A table to sit at.
Some messages cannot wait.
When someone writes that they are not safe, the AI is never asked. Their phone shows local crisis lines at once, and the care team's screen turns red.
A cry for help is always answered by a person.
Words matter too. In Korean, Catholics and Protestants even name God differently.
A glossary the pastor approves once keeps every translation in the church's own words, down to the tabs of the app: Mass for the parish, worship for the church across town.
During the service, a volunteer taps Next, and every phone in the pews follows along.
Koinonia counts languages, never names, and shows the welcome team where a group is arriving with no one to greet them.
lines.say: Koy-noh-nee-ah counts languages, never names, and shows the welcome team where a group is arriving with no one to greet them.

lines.text: Under the hood, Claude, served through the 0G Compute Network, summarises, drafts, translates, and checks. ElevenLabs gives every language a native voice.
lines.say: Under the hood, Claude, served through the zero G compute network, summarises, drafts, translates, and checks. ElevenLabs gives every language a native voice.

lines.text: Claude never sees personal details. Never writes Bible text. Never answers a crisis. And never sends a word without a person's approval.
Translation helps people hear. Koinonia helps them be heard: privacy on the phone, a meaning check before every reply, and a person for every cry for help.
lines.say: Translation helps people hear. Koy-noh-nee-ah helps them be heard: privacy on the phone, a meaning check before every reply, and a person for every cry for help.

lines.text: Koinonia. Every newcomer, heard.
